Suddenly, the jeep screeched to a halt. Zeidy looked outside, where an intimidating scene met his eyes. Arabs had blocked the road with large stones. Burning tires nearby filled the air with thick black smoke.

“We must turn around and go home,” said the driver. “It is too dangerous for us to continue.”

“No!” Zeidy firmly replied. The Rebbe had assured Zeidy’s group of shluchim that he was taking full responsibility for their safety. Confident in the Rebbe’s protection, Zeidy told the driver, “I’m not afraid. We won’t abandon our mission!”

The driver looked at him as if he was crazy. “You’re welcome to fulfill your mission another time, but I cannot take responsibility for your safety.”

Zeidy smiled. “Don’t worry,” he said. “The Rebbe is taking responsibility for us.”

“We are,” Zeidy and his friends emphatically replied.

The jeep rocked dangerously from side to side as it made its way over the boulders. As they continued driving, a group of Arabs began throwing rocks at the jeep. The vehicle shook violently as if it was caught in a hailstorm.

“We must turn back!” yelled the driver. “This situation is completely out of control!”

Zeidy didn’t back down. He had a shlichus to do. “If you turn back, I will get out and continue on my own.”

The Rebbe often said that Yidden need to stand strong and not give in to Goyim. Zeidy knew that he had an opportunity to show just that: Yidden were on their way to Shechem for a mitzvah, and nobody else would decide otherwise.

By now, the Arabs had surrounded the jeep. Left with no choice, the soldier on board opened his window and fired his weapon into the air. Poof! The crowd scattered instantly. The driver inched forward until they were clear of the rubble, and then sped up the highway with a deep sigh of relief.

Baruch Hashem, they arrived safely at the army base. With

shining faces, the devoted chassidim gave those soldiers a Purim to remember. The megillah was proudly read, graggers loudly whirled, and mishloach manos gratefully enjoyed. The army base in Shechem was permeated with the festive Purim spirit.

When the crew finally returned home, they called the Rebbe’s office to inform him of the day’s events.

After such an experience, they thought that the excitement was over. Boy, were they in for a surprise!

Hours later, at around 4:30 am, Zeidy was still awake— tuning in to the Rebbe’s Purim farbrengen. Eretz Yisroel time is seven hours ahead of New York, so Zeidy, together with many other bochurim, stayed

Suddenly, his eyes opened wide in disbelief. The Rebbe was telling his story!

“We just heard a story which happened today in Eretz Yisroel,” announced the Rebbe. The Rebbe proceeded to tell all the details, proudly comparing the chassidim to Mordechai HaYehudi. The megillah tells us, “ֹלא יִכְרַע וְֹלא יִׁשְּתַחֲוֶה—Mordechai didn’t bend or bow before Haman”. This group of shluchim, too, didn’t bow or give in to anything that tried disturbing their shlichus.

“In the end,” concluded the Rebbe, “neither the Yidden nor, lehavdil, the Arabs were harmed in any way. When a Yid remains firm and proud, we see clearly that no one gets hurt.”

Can you imagine the feeling of pride and joy that filled Zeidy’s yeshivah? Their very own shliach had given the Rebbe tremendous nachas! You can be sure that they did mivtzoyim with even more chayus, long after Purim was over.

Chayolim, we all have challenges. Going out on mivtzoyim can be hard. Remember this: You’re on a mission from the Rebbe, and he is right there with you. Be proud, and don’t let anything stand in your way! You’ll be amazed at how the difficulties can disappear.

“Purim Same’ach!” smiled the driver as he welcomed the unusual crew aboard his army jeep. Up climbed a group of passionate chassidim: two Bar Mitzvah boys, the gabbai of their shul, and our zeidy, R’ Yosef Yitzchok Gurevitch, who was then a bochur on shlichus in Eretz Yisroel. An Israeli soldier joined as well for added safety.
